title: Statistics
prerequisites: Mean, median and mode of ungrouped data.
Ability to plot points and draw a smooth curve.
Understanding of class intervals and class marks.

topics.title: Mean of Grouped Data
topics.quick_summary: The mean of grouped data is computed by the direct, assumed-mean or step-deviation method, all of which give the same answer.
topics.real_life: A school computing the average marks of five hundred students uses grouped data because listing every individual score would be unmanageable.

detailed.definition: For grouped data, the mean is Σfᵢxᵢ / Σfᵢ, where xᵢ is the class mark of the ith class and fᵢ its frequency. The step-deviation method uses uᵢ = (xᵢ − a)/h.
detailed.key_idea: All three methods are algebraically identical; only the arithmetic burden differs. The step-deviation method is preferred when the class marks are large and the class size is uniform.
detailed.working_principle: Grouping loses information: every observation in a class is treated as if it equalled the class mark. The computed mean is therefore an approximation, though a very good one.
applications: Direct method when the class marks are small.
Assumed-mean method when the class marks are large but class sizes are unequal.
Step-deviation method when class sizes are equal — it reduces the arithmetic most.

points: Class mark xᵢ = (upper limit + lower limit)/2.
Assumed mean: mean = a + Σfᵢdᵢ / Σfᵢ, where dᵢ = xᵢ − a.
Step-deviation: mean = a + h(Σfᵢuᵢ / Σfᵢ), where uᵢ = (xᵢ − a)/h.
All three methods give exactly the same answer.
mistakes: Using class limits instead of class marks as xᵢ.
Forgetting to multiply by h in the step-deviation method.
Choosing a value of a that is not a class mark, which complicates the arithmetic unnecessarily.
topics.memory_hook: 'Class mark times frequency, divided by total frequency' — the other two methods are just shortcuts.
topics.advanced: Grouping introduces a small bias when the distribution within classes is skewed. Sheppard's correction adjusts for this, though at school level the class-mark approximation is entirely adequate.

formulas.name: Mean of Grouped Data
formulas.formula: Direct: x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ/Σfᵢ;  Step-deviation: x̄ = a + h(Σfᵢuᵢ/Σfᵢ)
formulas.variables: xᵢ = class mark, fᵢ = frequency, a = assumed mean, h = class size, uᵢ = (xᵢ − a)/h.
formulas.when_to_use: For any grouped frequency distribution; step-deviation when class sizes are equal.
formulas.common_mistakes: Omitting the factor h in the step-deviation formula.
formulas.shortcut: Pick a as the class mark of the class with the highest frequency.

topics.title: Median, Mode and Ogives
topics.quick_summary: The median and mode of grouped data are found from the median and modal classes using interpolation formulas, and the median can also be read from an ogive.
topics.real_life: Median income is quoted rather than mean income precisely because a handful of very high earners would distort the average.

detailed.definition: The median class is the class in which the cumulative frequency first reaches or exceeds n/2. The modal class is the class with the highest frequency. An ogive is a cumulative frequency curve.
detailed.key_idea: Both formulas interpolate within a class rather than assuming the answer sits at a class boundary. This is why the cumulative frequency of the preceding class appears in the median formula.
detailed.working_principle: The point where the 'less than' and 'more than' ogives intersect gives the median directly, which is a useful graphical check on the computed value.
applications: Median is preferred for skewed data such as income or house prices.
Mode is used when the most common value is what matters, such as shoe sizes to stock.

points: Mode = l + [(f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)] × h.
Median class: the class where cumulative frequency first reaches n/2.
The two ogives intersect at the median.
mistakes: Using the frequency instead of the cumulative frequency of the preceding class in the median formula.
Taking the modal class as the one with the largest class mark instead of the largest frequency.
Failing to convert discontinuous classes into continuous ones before applying the formulas.
topics.memory_hook: 'Median needs cumulative frequency; Mode needs the neighbours of the tallest bar.'
topics.advanced: The median minimises the sum of absolute deviations while the mean minimises the sum of squared deviations. Each average is the optimal answer to a different question about the data.

formulas.name: Median of Grouped Data
formulas.variables: l = lower limit of the median class, n = total frequency, cf = cumulative frequency of the preceding class, f = frequency of the median class, h = class size.
formulas.when_to_use: For grouped data, especially when it is skewed.
formulas.common_mistakes: Using the frequency of the median class as cf.
formulas.shortcut: Build the cumulative frequency column first, before anything else.

formulas.name: Mode of Grouped Data
formulas.formula: Mode = l + [(f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)] × h
formulas.variables: l = lower limit of the modal class, f₁ = its frequency, f₀ = preceding frequency, f₂ = following frequency, h = class size.
formulas.when_to_use: For grouped data where the most frequent value is required.
formulas.common_mistakes: Mixing up f₀ and f₂, which lie on either side of the modal class.
formulas.shortcut: The modal class is simply the row with the highest frequency.
